content: PLS3, also known as Plastin-3, is a protein that is highly conserved across species and is encoded by the PLS3 gene located on the X chromosome in humans. Plastins belong to a family of actin-binding proteins that have been evolutionarily conserved throughout eukaryotic organisms. These proteins are expressed in most tissues of higher eukaryotes. In humans, two ubiquitously expressed plastin isoforms, known as L and T, have been identified. Additionally, Plastin-1, also referred to as Fimbrin, represents a third distinct isoform that is specifically expressed at high levels in the small intestine. The L isoform of plastin is exclusively expressed in hematopoietic cell lineages, whereas the T isoform is found in all other normal cells of solid tissues that possess replicative potential. These include fibroblasts, endothelial cells, epithelial cells, melanocytes, and similar cell types. The C-terminal region of the T-plastin and L-plastin proteins, consisting of 570 amino acids, shares 83% sequence identity. Furthermore, these proteins contain a potential calcium-binding site located near their N-terminal region. From a clinical perspective, mutations or defects in the PLS3 gene have been linked to osteoporosis and an increased risk of bone fractures in humans. Similar phenotypes have been observed in zebrafish models with PLS3 gene knockout.
